checkpoints.prompt: The EC2 compute workload used by the accounting team has a utilization rate of 10% on weekdays and 90% at the end of the month. Choose one approach to consider that will control costs based on operating hours while ensuring sufficient processing capacity at month-end.

choices.text: Measure actual usage at month-end and reassess the normal compute capacity.
choices.explanation: Measuring usage can reduce unnecessary compute capacity outside peak periods.

choices.text: Fix the compute capacity at the month-end peak level for the entire period.
choices.explanation: Because peak capacity is maintained even during low-utilization periods, this does not reassess capacity according to usage.

choices.text: Change to the largest instance without measuring usage.
choices.explanation: Scaling up without measurement makes it impossible to distinguish required performance from excess cost.

choices.text: Keep compute resources running continuously, even when unused, to avoid costs.
choices.explanation: Keeping resources running continuously eliminates the benefit of adjusting compute resources according to usage.

source.label: AWS: Six advantages of cloud computing

checkpoints.title: Provision when needed and reassess the required amount

checkpoints.prompt: An operations engineer found a dependency library on an application running on EC2 that needs to be updated. Choose the one correct party responsible for updating the library.

choices.text: Create a remediation plan as part of the customer-side OS and application updates.
choices.explanation: The customer is responsible for updating the EC2 guest OS and applications installed by the customer.

choices.text: Wait for AWS to update the application's dependency library.
choices.explanation: Responsibility for maintaining dependency libraries does not automatically transfer to AWS.

choices.text: Do not assign an update owner because responsibility is shared.
choices.explanation: Shared responsibility does not mean leaving ownership ambiguous.

choices.text: Ask the physical data center to patch the application.
choices.explanation: Protecting physical facilities and updating applications on EC2 are separate layers.

checkpoints.title: What AWS manages and what you must protect

checkpoints.prompt: A service owner wants the service to continue operating even if EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone stop simultaneously. Choose one architecture that separates the impact of a failure.

choices.text: Place redundant instances in a different AZ.
choices.explanation: Separating instances into a different AZ isolates them from failure domains common to a single AZ.

choices.text: Add more instances in the same AZ.
choices.explanation: Increasing the number of instances does not eliminate the common failure domain of the same AZ.

choices.text: Increase the CPU of the same instance.
choices.explanation: Changing capacity does not isolate an AZ failure.

choices.text: Change only the Region name to another name.
choices.explanation: Changing the name does not change the actual placement or failure domain.

checkpoints.title: Separate failure domains with Regions and AZs

checkpoints.prompt: There is a workload that experiences high load for only one hour each month, with a requirement to continue normal processing even if one AZ stops. Choose two correct starting points for comparison.

choices.text: Compare proposals that increase the required compute capacity only during high-load periods.
choices.explanation: This reflects time-based load variation in capacity planning.

choices.text: Compare the cost of redundancy across AZs, remaining capacity, and the effect of failure isolation.
choices.explanation: For a requirement to continue after an AZ stops, evaluating cost and remaining capacity is necessary.

choices.text: Choose the least expensive single AZ while ignoring the availability requirement.
choices.explanation: Ignoring the requirement in favor of cost alone fails to meet the necessary continuity.

choices.text: Fix the maximum capacity regardless of when the high load occurs.
choices.explanation: Fixing capacity at the peak alone does not allow the load-cost trade-off to be evaluated.

checkpoints.title: Compare load, failures, and costs separately

choices.text: Request computing resources when needed and adjust capacity according to usage.
choices.explanation: On-demand resources are used when needed and adjusted based on actual usage.

choices.text: Fix the maximum number of instances expected several years from now at the outset.
choices.explanation: Fixing the maximum does not allow adjustment based on usage.

choices.text: Change to the largest size without measuring usage.
choices.explanation: Without measurement, it is impossible to determine the required performance and unnecessary costs.

choices.text: Separate the data needed for resumption from unnecessary resources.
choices.explanation: Confirm the retention purpose and organize the costs and resumption requirements.

choices.text: Measure usage during normal periods and start with the required amount.
choices.explanation: Capacity can be determined based on actual usage.

choices.text: Reduce the computing resources added after aggregation is complete.
choices.explanation: This can reduce unnecessary operation during periods of low load.

choices.text: Run all resources at maximum capacity at all times.
choices.explanation: Constantly running at maximum capacity does not reflect load fluctuations in the cost.

choices.text: Do not check the conditions or limits for automatic adjustment.

choices.text: Updating the EC2 guest OS installed by the user.

choices.text: The user should plan the update and perform operational checks.
choices.explanation: The guest OS is managed by the user.

choices.text: Responsibility for physical facility security measures differs from responsibility for updating the guest OS.
choices.explanation: AWS is responsible for the physical infrastructure, while the user is responsible for the guest OS.

choices.text: Because it is an OS on AWS, the user does not need to update it.
choices.explanation: Updating the EC2 guest OS is not automatically transferred to AWS.

choices.text: The user's scope of operations varies by service.
choices.explanation: The layers that are managed differ by service.

choices.text: The user verifies who can access the data stored in S3.
choices.explanation: Data permissions are the user's responsibility.

choices.text: With a managed service, the user no longer needs any security settings.
choices.explanation: Responsibility for data and access permissions remains.

choices.text: Updating the EC2 guest OS and managing entry to and exit from AWS facilities are handled by the same party.
choices.explanation: The user is responsible for the guest OS, while AWS is responsible for physical facilities.

finalQuestions.prompt: Regarding shared responsibility for a team using S3 and EC2, select two incorrect explanations.
finalQuestions.title: Responsibilities That Remain Even with Managed Services

choices.text: An AZ is an isolated location within a single Region.
choices.explanation: An AZ is a fault-isolation unit within a Region.

choices.text: A single AZ is a geographical unit that combines multiple Regions.
choices.explanation: An AZ does not combine multiple Regions; it is located within a Region.

choices.text: A Region is a geographical unit where resources are placed.
choices.explanation: Resources are placed by selecting a Region.

choices.text: If one server fails, the other may serve as a backup.
choices.explanation: During a single-server failure, another server in the same AZ may remain available.

choices.text: If the entire AZ fails, both servers may be affected.
choices.explanation: They share the common failure scope of the same AZ.

choices.text: Having two servers does not guarantee eliminating the impact of an AZ failure.
choices.explanation: Increasing the number of servers does not eliminate the common failure scope of the AZ.

choices.text: Simply adding AZs automatically replicates data to another Region.
choices.explanation: AZ distribution and cross-Region replication are separate settings.

choices.text: Verify that traffic flows to a healthy processing destination.
choices.explanation: The communication path is also necessary, not just the placement.

choices.text: Verify that the required data remains reachable during an AZ-a outage.
choices.explanation: Processing cannot continue if dependent data is unavailable.

choices.text: Because the placement is split, do not verify the processing capacity of the remaining resources.
choices.explanation: The remaining capacity after the failure must be validated.

choices.text: If multiple AZs are used, replication to another Region is also complete.
choices.explanation: Distributing resources across AZs does not mean replicating them to another Region.

finalQuestions.prompt: After distributing the workload across two AZs, verify preparedness for an AZ-a outage. Select two incorrect judgments.

choices.text: Who would be affected if the site went down, and how long could they wait?
choices.explanation: The impact of an outage and the acceptable duration become continuity requirements.

choices.text: Should we maximize the number of instances regardless of the objective?
choices.explanation: The number of instances alone cannot determine the need or the scope of an outage.

choices.text: If it is in the cloud, should we avoid checking the impact of an outage?
choices.explanation: Even in the cloud, the business impact and acceptable duration must be confirmed.

finalQuestions.prompt: The operations team is reviewing the system architecture in preparation for an outage that could bring down the order site. Select one question that should be confirmed with the business team before comparing candidates.
finalQuestions.title: Availability Assessment

choices.text: With proposal A, all three instances stop.
choices.explanation: This is because all three instances share the failure domain of AZ-a.

choices.text: With proposal B, one instance remains in AZ-b, but verify whether it can process the required amount.
choices.explanation: Verify not only the number of remaining instances but also the remaining capacity.

choices.text: Because proposal A has more instances, at least one remains.
choices.explanation: When the same AZ stops, all three instances are affected.

choices.text: Because one instance remains with proposal B, checking the required processing volume is unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Having one instance remain does not guarantee processing capacity.

finalQuestions.prompt: Proposal A has three instances in AZ-a, while proposal B has one instance each in AZ-a and AZ-b. Select two correct comparisons of processing capacity after AZ-a stops.
finalQuestions.title: Comparing instance count and placement

choices.text: Consider capacity measures for congestion and protection against an AZ failure separately.
choices.explanation: Capacity and failure scope are different objectives.

choices.text: Increasing computing power can prevent an AZ failure regardless of placement.
choices.explanation: Increasing capacity does not eliminate the shared scope of an AZ failure.

choices.text: With multiple AZs, there is no need to consider operational burden or cost.
choices.explanation: The burden of additional resources and operations must also be compared.

choices.text: Explain for each architecture which failures it prevents and what risks remain.
choices.explanation: Making residual risks explicit enables comparison.

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Separate usage volume, responsibility boundaries, and failure scope, then choose a cloud configuration that meets the requirements.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Distinguish usage volume, the layers under responsibility, and failure scope, and explain why a cloud configuration is selected.

blocks.label: Learning Objectives
blocks.text: Explain why usage should be adjusted based on on-demand pricing and pay-as-you-go billing.

blocks.label: Learning Objectives
blocks.text: Determine the responsibilities of AWS and the user based on the services used and the layer being managed.

blocks.label: Learning Objectives
blocks.text: Explain the Region/AZ hierarchy and the shared scope of failures.

blocks.label: Learning Objectives
blocks.text: Compare configurations while distinguishing load, failures, and costs.

blocks.label: Prepare resources when needed and adjust the required amount
blocks.text: On-demand means using resources such as compute, storage, and networking when they are needed. Instead of fixing capacity for the maximum load from the outset, measure actual usage and adjust capacity.

blocks.label: Prepare resources when needed and adjust the required amount
blocks.text: Scaling out means increasing the number of instances, scaling in means decreasing the number of instances, and scaling up means increasing the capability of one instance. Being able to change something and having it change automatically are different, so automation requires conditions and limits.

blocks.label: Prepare resources when needed and adjust the required amount
blocks.text: Stopping compute resources does not necessarily eliminate charges for disks or stored data that remain. Check the purpose, retention period, and cost for each resource.

steps.label: Prepare resources when needed and adjust the required amount

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: Run a small internal aggregation in the cloud on weekdays, with an increase only at the end of the month.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Measure the processing volume on weekdays.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Increase compute capacity only at the end of the month.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Reduce unnecessary compute resources after processing and retain the required data.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can assess peak handling and normal-period costs separately.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Moving to the cloud will lower costs without any action.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Unused compute resources, storage, and data transfer may still incur costs, so review usage and retained resources.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Distinguish between being able to use resources when needed and automatic adjustment.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Check costs by factor, such as compute, storage, and data transfer.

sources.label: AWS: Six advantages of cloud computing

blocks.label: What AWS manages and what you protect yourself
blocks.text: The shared responsibility model shows the boundary between the infrastructure managed by AWS and the configurations and data managed by the customer.

blocks.label: What AWS manages and what you protect yourself
blocks.text: AWS manages the facilities, physical equipment, and service infrastructure. The customer manages data exposure, permissions, and network settings.

blocks.label: What AWS manages and what you protect yourself
blocks.text: For EC2, the customer updates the guest OS and installed applications. For S3, the customer does not manage the OS but verifies the access permissions for the data.

steps.label: What AWS manages and what you protect yourself

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: A vulnerable dependency library was found in an EC2 web application.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Identify that the target is an application on the guest OS, not the physical infrastructure.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Create an update plan and perform validation on the user side.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Also check the permissions and exposure scope.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Do not confuse AWS physical protection with the user's OS and application maintenance.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: AWS updates all resources on AWS.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Responsibility differs by service and layer; the EC2 guest OS and user settings remain the user's responsibility.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Identify the service name and the layer where the problem occurs.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Consider the physical infrastructure, OS, application, and data permissions separately.

blocks.label: Separate failure scopes using Regions and AZs
blocks.text: A Region is a geographic unit where resources are placed. An AZ is an isolated location within a single Region, and resources placed in the same AZ may share a common failure domain.

blocks.label: Separate failure scopes using Regions and AZs
blocks.text: Increasing the number of instances within the same AZ can protect against a single-instance failure, but it does not separate the failure domain of the AZ as a whole. Distributing resources across different AZs separates the failure domains.

blocks.label: Separate failure scopes using Regions and AZs
blocks.text: Switching Regions in the console does not automatically move or replicate existing resources. Replication to another Region requires service-specific configuration.

steps.label: Separate failure scopes using Regions and AZs

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: Assume that two instances in the same AZ stop simultaneously.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Distinguish between a single-instance failure and an AZ failure.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Place the required processing in another AZ.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Verify the remaining capacity and the reachability of dependent data.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can evaluate availability by separating failure domains, not just by increasing the number of instances.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Adding AZs automatically replicates to another Region.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: AZ distribution and cross-Region replication are separate designs and configurations.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: An AZ is a fault-isolation unit within a Region.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Placing resources in different AZs alone does not guarantee surviving capacity or data availability.

blocks.label: Compare load, failure, and cost separately
blocks.text: Load mitigation is a design that provides the processing capacity needed, while failure mitigation is a design that separates resources from a common failure domain. Because their objectives differ, simply increasing the number of instances does not satisfy both requirements.

blocks.label: Compare load, failure, and cost separately
blocks.text: If the requirement is to continue operating even when one AZ is unavailable, compare the cost of redundancy across AZs, the remaining capacity, and reachability to dependencies. If the high load lasts only a short time, also compare an option that increases capacity only for that period.

blocks.label: Compare load, failure, and cost separately
blocks.text: Choose an architecture based not only on the lowest price, but also on who would be affected, how long they can wait, and what risks would remain.

steps.label: Compare load, failure, and cost separately

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: The workload becomes high for only one hour per month, and processing must continue after one AZ stops.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Compare capacity options for the peak period.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Compare the cost and benefits of redundancy across AZs.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Verify the remaining processing volume after the AZ is stopped.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Explain the trade-offs among load, availability, and cost.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Placing one high-performance instance makes the system more resilient to an AZ failure.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Capacity and failure scope are separate considerations, and AZ failures require distributing resources across locations.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Treat load, failures, and cost as separate decision factors.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Do not choose the least expensive configuration that fails to meet the requirements.
